longformArticle.deck: A source-aware account of receipt legends, timestamp anomalies, point-of-sale trust, and proof-of-purchase memory.
opening: A receipt is a trusted proof-of-purchase object, so a contradictory timestamp can carry far more narrative force than a generic technical warning.
This record keeps one incident chain while isolating the later cultural amplification that followed it.

storyBody.heading: New-Year Checkout, Normal Until One Field Failed
paragraphs: On New Year’s Day 2001, a routine checkout sequence in convenience-store systems became a public records memory that still echoes in modern rumor culture. In several 7-Eleven stores, receipts printed a year of 1901 for purchases, creating a direct contradiction between what people saw on paper and the actual date.
What makes this a single-event record is the tight chain: one documented timestamp anomaly, one operational effect, one repair window, and one long afterlife of reused narrative shape.

The event started as a normal transaction loop: a customer paid, a cashier initiated a sale, and the receipt printed what customers typically trust as proof-of-purchase details. In that context, the receipt is usually treated as a complete object because it bundles date, items, total, and merchant context into one compact artifact.
That normalcy matters. The same store, same staff, same checkout flow, and same customer expectations were all in place when one field slipped out of its expected range.

storyBody.heading: The Impossible Receipt Year
paragraphs: When the chain broke, the date on some receipts read Jan. 1, 1901 instead of 2001 during the January 1 transactions. For customers paying by card, this could interrupt the POS path because the receipt line fed directly into a transaction control routine used by the chain’s payment stack.

The contradiction was immediately intelligible because it was visible, singular, and hard to dismiss. A receipt that says one year while all other context feels current is not an abstract theory; it is a concrete, witnessed artifact mismatch.

storyBody.heading: Credit Path Disruption and Immediate Customer Impact
paragraphs: The disruption did not only confuse people’s trust. Stores reported that card processing could fail while cash alternatives still moved.

This is why the aftereffect became memorable in operational terms. In many systems, people do not notice a backend fault until it blocks a familiar action. Here, they did: a purchase that should be instantly settled was blocked at proof stage, even though the transaction was not physically impossible.

storyBody.heading: Manual Backup Instead of Total Outage
paragraphs: Operations teams shifted to backup handling so business could continue. That shift kept store activity moving while engineers investigated the defect. In effect, this phase shows a classic operational split: visible trust artifact failed, but the organization’s fallback sequence preserved function.
In the story record, this is the action-and-evidence phase. We can see: report, local containment, manual alternatives, technical investigation.

storyBody.heading: Patch Night and the Return of Transaction Continuity
paragraphs: By the following day, a software patch restored normal date output for the affected POS path. That action did not erase the incident but separated it into two clear tracks: the technical remedy and the memory track.
The technical track ended with corrected receipts; the memory track started where the contradiction had already moved into public storytelling.

storyBody.heading: Why This Failed Date Became a Repeat Legend Motif
paragraphs: Modern records folklore repeatedly revives moments where an evidence artifact appears internally inconsistent. This one gave people a template: “a trusted proof object with a missing certainty point becomes proof of a larger hidden problem.”

That template is why similar odd date receipts, blank fields, and hard-to-verify store records keep returning in later digital-era caution tales. One event stayed bounded in time, but the structural lesson travels with it.
